recognition.transcript: Three towns share a council of 15 seats. Ash has 4,000 people, Birch has 9,000, and Cedar has 26,000.
A careful rule, which we will rebuild together in a few minutes, splits the seats like this: Ash gets 2, Birch gets 3, and Cedar gets 10.
Now the council grows to 16 seats. Nobody moves, nobody is born, and no population changes at all. There is simply one more seat to hand out, under exactly the same rule. What happens to Ash?
Ash drops from two seats to one. Birch and Cedar each gain a seat. The council got bigger, and the smallest town came out with less.

This is called the Alabama Paradox, after a real state that met it in 1880. Nothing in the arithmetic is wrong, and every step we take will be exact. The trouble lives in a deeper question: how should fair fractions become whole seats?
We will rebuild the rule that did this, see exactly why it happens, meet the rules invented to avoid it, and end with a theorem about which promises no rule can keep together.
Start with what 'fair' would mean if seats could be cut into pieces. Together, the towns hold 39,000 people. 15 seats for 39,000 people is one seat for every 2,600 people.

So each town's fair share of seats is its population divided by 2,600. Ash's share is 1.54 seats. Birch's is 3.46. Cedar's is exactly 10. Mathematicians call this exact number the quota. I will call it the town's share.
But a seat is a person. Nobody can sit in point five four of a chair. Each town needs a whole number of seats, and the whole numbers have to add up to exactly 15.
The obvious move is to round each share to the nearest whole number. At 15 seats, that works, because 2 + 3 + 10 is 15. Will rounding to the nearest always give the right total?
No. At 14 seats, the shares are 1.44, 3.23 and 9.33. Every one rounds down and the council is a seat short. At 16 seats, every share rounds up and we hand out 17.
Rounding each town on its own forgets the one thing that ties them together: the total. So every rule needs a second idea, a way to settle the seats that rounding gets wrong.

There are two classic families. One keeps the shares fixed and compares what is left over. The other changes how many people count as a seat until ordinary rounding adds up. The paradox lives in the first family.

Here is the first family's most natural rule. It carries Alexander Hamilton's name, and it is also called the method of largest remainders. Give every town the whole part of its share. Then hand out the seats that remain, one each, to the towns with the largest leftover fractions.
Call the fraction after the whole part the town's tail. At 15 seats, the whole parts are 1, 3 and 10. That makes 14 seats, so one seat is left over.
The tails are .54 for Ash, .46 for Birch, and nothing at all for Cedar. Who gets the leftover seat?
Ash has the largest tail, so Ash gets it. Two seats for Ash, three for Birch, ten for Cedar, the allocation we started with.

This rule comes with a real guarantee: the shares add up to the house, and the whole parts are whole, so the tails always add up to a whole number, which is exactly the number of leftover seats. Every tail is less than one, so there are fewer leftover seats than towns, and no town can receive two of them.

So every town ends up with its share rounded down or rounded up. Call that the quota promise. Hamilton's rule keeps it at every house size. Judged one size at a time, it looks perfectly fair. The trouble only appears when we compare two sizes.
Now add the 16th seat. Every share grows because the same people now divide more seats. Ash's share becomes 1.64, Birch's 3.69, and Cedar's 10.67.
The whole parts are still 1, 3 and 10. That is 14 again, so this time two seats are left over.
Ash's tail is now 0.64, Birch's is 0.69, Cedar's is 0.67. Which two towns get the two leftover seats?
Birch and Cedar. A moment ago, Ash had the largest tail. Now it has the smallest. So the result is 1, 4, 11. Ash's share went up and Ash lost a seat.

Look how close the race is! Measured in thirty-ninths of a seat, the tails are twenty-five, twenty-seven and twenty-six. Ash misses by a single thirty-ninth. But a near miss does not explain anything. The real question is why the order of the tails changed at all.

Picture each share as a hand on a dial. One full turn of the hand is one whole seat. Watch Ash's dial as the council grows from no seats to 15. Each time the hand passes the top, the whole part ticks up by one and the tail starts again from zero. Birch's and Cedar's dials show their own shares at 15 seats in the same way.

Adding one seat to the council increases each town's share by that town's fraction of the total population. Ash has 4,000 of the 39,000 people, so one more seat turns Ash's hand by 4/39 of a turn. Birch's hand turns 9/39. Cedar's turns 26/39, two-thirds of the way around.
At 15 seats, Ash's hand is ahead of Birch's, and Cedar's points straight up at zero. Turn every hand by its own step. Which hand ends up in front?

Birch's. Ash's hand creeps forward. Birch's moves more than twice as far and passes it. Cedars swings two-thirds of a turn and passes it too. Nothing about Ash got worse. The other hands simply moved faster.

So here is the mechanism. Hamilton's rule hands out leftover seats by rank, and the rank is decided by tails. Tails do not grow steadily with the house. They wrap around, each at its own speed. A slow hand, like a small town's, can be overtaken from one house size to the next while its whole part stays put. That is how a share can rise while its seats fall.
Add one more seat, 17 in all. Does Ash get its seat back?
It does. The whole parts become one. Three and eleven. Two seats are left over, and the largest tails now belong to Birch and Ash. Two, four, eleven.

So the paradox is not a slide. It comes and goes as the hands turn. Run Hamilton's rule for every council from one seat to a hundred. That is 99 editions of a single seat. Five of them take a seat away from somebody, and every time it is ash.

History found the same thing. After the 1880 census, the chief clerk of the census office, a man named Seton, worked out Hamilton apportionments for every house size from 275 to 350. Alabama received eight seats in a house of 299 and seven in a house of 300.
Seton reported it to Congress in a letter which Peyton Young quotes: "Such a result as this is to me conclusive proof that the process employed in obtaining it is defective."
Those were alternative calculations, not a real house that grew and took a seat away. But they showed that the danger was real.
Now the second family. Go back to 15 seats. Divide each population by 2,600, the exact number of people per seat, and drop every tail. You get one, three, and ten. 14 seats, one short.

Thomas Jefferson's rule keeps the rounding and changes the yardstick instead. It always rounds down, and it adjusts how many people count as one seat. To hand out one more seat, should that number go up or down?

Down. Fewer people per seat means every town has more seats worth of people. Slide the yardstick from 2,600 down to 2,300. Ash now has 1.74 seats worth, Birch 3.91 and Cedar 11.3. Drop the tails and you get 1, 3, 11. 15 seats exactly.
Any yardstick above 2,250 and up to about 2,364 gives the same answer. That is Jefferson's rule. Choose the number of people per seat that makes the whole parts add up to the house.
Notice what changed. Every town is measured with the same yardstick, and no town's tail is ever compared with another's.

Look at the same slide another way. As the yardstick falls, each town gains its next seat at a definite moment. Cedar gains its first seat when the yardstick reaches 26,000, its second at 13,000, its third at about 8,667. Those are 26,000 divided by 1, 2 and 3.

Ash's seats open at 4,000, then 2,000. Birch's open at 9,000, 4,500 and 3,000. Call each of these a signpost. Put every signpost on one list, largest first, and Jefferson's rule just reads the list from the top. 15 seats means the first 15 signposts.
The first 15 signposts give 1, 3, 11. Whose signpost comes 16th?
Birch's fourth seat at 2,250. 16 seats gives 1, 4, 11. And the 17th signpost, Cedar's 12th, gives 1, 4, 12.
And this is why the family can never take a seat back. 16 seats are the first 16 signposts, and the first 15 are among them. A bigger house just reads further down the same list.

Precisely. That needs a single order on the list. At 2,000 people per seat, Ash's second signpost and Cedar's 13th are exactly tied, so a council of 18 would need a tie rule. Fix the order of tied signposts once and keep it as the house grows. Our 15, 16 and 17 seat allocations stop before this tie.
Jefferson's rule never takes a seat back. But look at Cedar at 15 seats. It gets 11. Does that keep the quota promise?
It does not. Cedar's share at 15 seats is exactly 10, so rounded down or up, it is still 10. Jefferson gives it 11. And the extra seat came from Ash, which gets one seat for a share of 1.54.

That is no accident. Rounding down throws away less than a seat from every town, but the same sliver is a bigger slice of a small town. At 2,300 people per seat, Ash throws away 42.5% of its count. Cedar throws away less than 3%. Jefferson's rule leans toward large towns.
History shows the lean. In the apportionment after the 1830 census, made with Jefferson's rule, New York's exact share was 38.593 seats. Peyton Young's table records that it received 40.
So the two families trade flaws. Hamilton's rule keeps the quota promise, but can take a seat back. Jefferson's rule never takes a seat back, but can break the quota promise.
Jefferson rounds every quotient down. Change where the rounding happens and you get the rest of the family, each one built the same way, with a sliding yardstick and one list of signposts.

John Quincy Adams proposed rounding up instead. Now any piece of a quotient earns a whole seat, so the lean flips towards small towns. At 15 seats, Adams gives 2, 4 and 9. Cedar falls below its share of exactly 10.
Between always down and always up sits the compromise, round to the nearest. What does that give at 15 seats?

2, 3, 10. The same as Hamilton. This is Daniel Webster's rule. At 16 seats, it gives 2, 4, 10. And at 17, 2, 4, 11. Nobody ever loses a seat. In our three towns, Webster does what we hoped Hamilton would do.

One more relative is worth knowing, because it became the law for the United States House in 1941. It is called the Huntington Hill Method. Between 1 and 2, it rounds up once a quotient passes the square root of 1 times 2, about 1.41. For our towns, it agrees with Webster at 15, 16 and 17 seats.

Each pair of neighbouring whole numbers gets its own threshold: the square root of the two multiplied together. Between 2 and 3 it is the square root of 6, about 2.45. Between 3 and 4 the square root of 12, about 3.46. Each one sits a little below Webster's halfway mark, and closer to it the higher you go. But between 0 and 1 the threshold is the square root of 0, which is 0.

So whenever there are enough seats to go round, Hill's rule gives every town at least one seat, and that can break the quota promise even with three towns. At three seats it gives each town one seat, though Cedar's share is exactly two. Every rule in this family reads one list of signposts, so none of them ever takes a seat back, and every one of them can break the quota promise for some map of towns.
Webster's rule looks like the best of both families. Can it ever break the quota promise?

Not with three towns. Balinski and Young proved it. Here is why. To break the promise, a town must end a whole seat or more below its share. So its quotient is below its share, and the yardstick sits above the exact one. Then every other quotient is below its share, and rounding to the nearest adds at most half a seat. So the other two towns end less than one seat above their shares, too little to cover the missing seat. Turned around, the same reasoning rules out a whole seat too many. With four towns, it can happen.

Take four towns of 2,000, 5,000, 8,000 and 27,000 people, sharing 14 seats. The biggest town's share is exactly nine. The three small shares are 0.67, 1.67 and 2.67. And rounding to the nearest lifts each one by a third of a seat. Three small towns, three thirds, one whole seat. Rounding everything to the nearest, hands out 15 seats. One too many.

To take one away, the yardstick must grow until some town's quotient drops below its halfway mark. The big town's halfway mark comes first. Its quotient falls below 8.5, while the small towns still round up. Webster gives 1, 2, 3 and 8. The town whose share is exactly 9 gets 8.
So even the best divisor rule can break the quota promise. Is there any rule that keeps the quota promise and never takes a seat back?
Jefferson broke the quota promise at 15 seats by giving Cedar its 11th seat. Suppose a rule refuses any seat that would lift a town above its share rounded up. Who gets the 15th seat instead?

Birch. Michel Bolinski and Peyton Young published exactly this rule in 1974 and called it the Quota Method. Here it is in a simple form: hand out seats one at a time from the top of Jefferson's list. Before giving a town its next seat, check that the seat would not lift it above its share rounded up at the new house size. If it would, skip that signpost for now and go to the next one.

At 15 seats, Cedar already has 10, and its share is exactly 10, so it is skipped. The next signpost is Birch's fourth at 2250, which beats Ash's second at 2000. The result is 1, 4, 10. At 16 seats, Cedar's ceiling rises to 11, and it gets its seat.

Each house is the previous house plus one seat, so nobody ever loses one. And Bolinsky and Young's theorem says the skipping never strands a town below its share rounded down either. Both promises, at every house size. Here is one way to see why that is true.

Lay each town's seats along the house sizes as a row of tiles. Every added seat raises a town's share by its fraction of the people, so each tile is as long as the stretch of house sizes it takes to earn one whole seat. Ash's tiles are nine and three quarters long, birches four and a third, and cedars one and a half.

Now slide a marker along the house sizes. A town's share, rounded down, counts the tiles the marker has passed completely. Rounded up, it counts the tiles the marker has entered. So the quota promise says that every tile the marker has passed is already handed out, and no tile it has not entered is.

And Jefferson's list is these tiles in the order they end. A seat's signpost is the population divided by the seat number. So the bigger the signpost, the sooner that seat's tile ends. At every house size, the quota method takes the entered tiles nobody holds yet and hands out the one that ends soonest.

Could a past tile ever be left out? Suppose one were. Go back to the last moment the rule handed out a tile that ends later than the missing one, or to the very start if it never did. Every tile handed out since then, and the missing tile too, had not been entered at that moment, or the rule would have picked a tile ending sooner, and every one of them ends by now.

So all those tiles fit inside the stretch from that moment to now, and there is one more of them than seats added in the stretch. But each town's row fits at most the stretch times its fraction of the people, and the fractions add up to one. So a stretch never holds more whole tiles than the seats added across it, and no past tile is ever left out. The quota method never hands out a tile before the marker enters it, so it keeps the quota promise at every house size.

Notice that the quota method gives 1, 4, 10 at 15 seats, while Hamilton gives 2, 3, 10. Both keep the quota promise. That promise can allow more than one answer, and different rules choose differently.
So far, no population has changed. Real towns grow and shrink, which suggests a third promise: a town that did not shrink should never lose a seat to a town that did not grow.
Take a later census: Ash shrinks to 3,900. Birch grows to 9,500. Cedar grows a little, to 26,100. The council stays at 16 seats.
Before the census, Hamilton gave 1, 4, 11. What does it give now?
2, 4, 10. The new shares are 1.58, 3.85 and 10.57. Ash's tail now beats Cedar's. So Cedar, which grew, loses a seat to Ash, which shrank.

Divisor rules cannot do this. Every signpost is a population divided by a fixed number. When a town grows, all of its signposts get bigger, so they can pass the signposts of towns that did not grow, but never fall behind them. When a town shrinks, all of its signposts get smaller, so they can fall behind the signposts of towns that did not shrink, but never pass them.

Watch Jefferson's list through the census, one town at a time. Birch grows, and its fourth signpost passes Cedar's eleventh. Cedar grows a little, and its thirteenth signpost, once tied with Ash's second, moves ahead of it. Ash shrinks, and only the values on its cards change. Its first signpost falls from 4,000 to 3,900, and no card moves. At 16 seats, the list still gives 1, 4, 11, before the census, and after it.
That is a strong reason to prefer divisor rules. But they cannot always keep the quota promise. Could some cleverer rule keep the quota promise and the population promise together?

Belinsky and Young proved in 1982 that the answer is no, with one extra assumption: a town with strictly more people than another must never get fewer seats. A recent paper by Paul Goltz, Dominic Peters and Ariel Procaccia proves the answer is still no without that assumption, for any rule that always gives the same answer to the same question.
Their proof needs more than our three towns, because with three towns, Webster's rule keeps both promises. It uses a city and four villages sharing ten seats, and we can follow all of it.

One city of 824 people and four villages of 44 people each share 10 seats. The city's share is 8.24 and each village's is 0.44. So the quota promise lets the city have eight seats or nine. Which choice is safe?

Neither. Suppose the city gets nine. Then the last seat goes to one village. Call it the fifth. Now let only the fifth village grow, to 222 people. The city's share falls to 6.99, so it can have at most seven seats. The fifth village's share is 1.88, so it can have at most two. That leaves at least one seat for the other three villages.

So some village with an unchanged population goes from no seats to one, while the city, also unchanged, drops from nine seats to seven or fewer. The city did not shrink, and it lost seats to a village that did not grow. The population promise is broken.

Suppose instead the city gets eight. Then two villages get one seat each. Call them the fourth and fifth. This time, shrink the other two villages to a single person each. The city's share rises to 9.02, so it needs at least nine seats. Only one seat is left for the fourth and fifth villages, so one of them drops to zero. That village did not shrink, and it lost its seat to a city that did not grow.

Both choices fail. So no rule that keeps the quota promise can keep the population promise for every map of five towns. And the same trick works with more. With three towns, Webster's rule keeps both. With four, without the extra assumption, nobody knew as of that paper.

The same paper shows what a lottery can add. If the rule may draw lots, it can keep the quota promise, never take a seat back, and give every town exactly its share on average. But even a lottery cannot keep the quota promise and the population promise together.
Here is the whole map. Hamilton's rule keeps the quota promise, but it can take a seat back when the house grows, and it can punish a town for growing.

Jefferson, Adams, Webster and Hill never take a seat back and never punish growth, but each can break the quota promise. The quota method of Belinsky and Young keeps the quota promise and never takes a seat back, and the theorem says it must break the population promise for some map.
Here is one to try yourself. Under Webster's rule, suppose cedar grows while ash and birch stay exactly the same, and the council stays at 15 seats. Can ash ever gain a seat?

No. Cedars signposts all get bigger, while Ashes and Birches keep exactly the same values. As Cedars climb past some of them, those are pushed down the list, but none can move up. So the cut-off for 15 seats can only rise, and any signpost of Ashes that was below it stays below it. Ash can keep its seats or lose some, but it can never gain one.

Back where we started. Ash lost a seat when the council grew. Not because anyone slipped in the arithmetic, but because Hamilton's rule ranks tails, and tails wrap around at different speeds. Fair fractions are easy. Fair whole numbers force a choice. And now you know exactly which promises can be kept together and which cannot.
